For most Black Americans, both Black and standard English are part of who we are; our English is, in this sense, larger than many white people’s. In “The Souls of Black Folk,” W.E.B. Du Bois wrote, “I sit with Shakespeare and he winces not … I summon Aristotle and Aurelius and what soul I will, and they come all graciously with no scorn nor condescension.” On a less exalted level, a great many Black people toggle endlessly between standard and Black English, day in and day out — we code-switch. Now it turns out that for the last eight years, another major book was in the works: "W. E. B. Du Bois: Biography of a Race, 1868-1919" (Henry Holt & Company, New York, $35), a 735-page tome, described by Dr. Lewis in his preface as a project that "often rendered me unaware of the routine of daily life." Du Bois died in 1963 at the age of 95, and the research involved travel over three continents, inquiry into 28 archives and 99 library collections and interviews with more than 150 people. "And alas," Dr. Lewis said recently, "all this for what it turns out is only volume one." But "Du Bois" -- a candidate for the National Book Award in nonfiction -- is a powerfully thorough book that because its subject was such a extraordinary leader, so central to the political controversies around him, it compels a reappraisal of the post-Civil War era. Du Bois is perhaps best known in the civil rights movement for his insistence on full equality for his fellow blacks, as opposed to the accommodative policies of Booker T. Washington. But Dr. Lewis's book reveals much more about Du Bois as political strategist. In 1911, for example, when Woodrow Wilson, then Governor of New Jersey, prepared to enter the Presidential race, he asked Du Bois to influence blacks to depart from their traditional Republican stance and vote Democratic. **Justification:** The passage describes Du Bois as a "scholar" through the context of a biography being written about him, highlighting his intellectual contributions and his role in social and political theory. Ghana's Pan-Africanist foreign policy was evident last October, when the Government declared five days of mourning in honor of Samora M. Machel, the Mozambique leader who was killed in a plane crash in South Africa. Seeds of African Independence In the first half of this century, Du Bois organized five Pan-African congresses, meetings that planted the seeds for the crop of independent nations that sprang up in Africa in the 1960's. Almost a quarter of a century after Du Bois's death, the Pan-Africanist outlook can be seen in the joint pressure mounted by Africans and black Americans to win majority rule for South-West African, known as Namibia, and South Africa. Pan-Africanists have also encountered setbacks. For now, Du Bois's ideal of a United States of Africa seems far out of reach. One symbol of modern Africa's nationalist rivalries was Nigeria's abrupt expulsion - enforced with pistols and whips - of a million illegal workers from Ghana in 1983. The scholarship on Reconstruction is vast and comprehensive. But my touchstone for thinking about the period continues to be W.E.B. Du Bois’s “Black Reconstruction,” published in 1935 after years of painstaking research that was often inhibited by segregation and the racism of Southern institutions of higher education. I return to Du Bois, even as I read more recent work, because he offers a framework that is useful, I think, for analyzing the struggle for democracy in our own time. The central conceit of Du Bois’s landmark study — whose full title is “Black Reconstruction: An Essay Toward a History of the Part Which Black Folk Played in the Attempt to Reconstruct Democracy in America, 1860-1880” — is that the period was a grand struggle between “two theories of the future of America,” rooted in the relationship of American labor to American democracy. “What were to be the limits of democratic control in the United States?” Du Bois asks. “Was the rule of the mass of Americans to be unlimited, and the right to rule extended to all men regardless of race and color?” And if not, he continues, “How would property and privilege be protected?”

**Justification:** The passage explicitly refers to Du Bois's "Black Reconstruction" as a "landmark study" and discusses his "scholarship" and the "framework" it offers for analyzing democracy.
